whatIs.title: What is AI Governance?
whatIs.p1: AI governance refers to the structured framework of principles, policies, operational controls, and accountability mechanisms that guide how artificial intelligence systems are designed, deployed, monitored, and corrected.
whatIs.p2: It ensures that AI systems operate in alignment with legal standards, ethical norms, institutional objectives, and long-term societal interests. Governance is not a single compliance checkbox; it is a continuous lifecycle discipline.

bias.title: Bias & Discrimination Risks
bias.description: Without governance, AI models can reinforce historical biases, leading to unfair credit decisions, exclusionary outcomes, or systemic discrimination.

opacity.title: Opacity & Explainability Gaps
opacity.description: Black-box models undermine trust. Governance frameworks require transparent documentation, explainability techniques, and interpretability controls.

regulatory.title: Regulatory & Legal Exposure
regulatory.description: Regulatory environments increasingly demand traceability, auditability, and documented risk controls for AI systems.

accountability.title: Accountability
accountability.description: Clear ownership of model decisions, defined responsibility structures, and escalation mechanisms for high-risk AI systems.

traceability.title: Traceability
traceability.description: Full documentation of model versions, training data sources, validation procedures, and deployment changes across the lifecycle.

monitoring.title: Monitoring & Risk Management
monitoring.description: Continuous oversight of model drift, performance degradation, and emerging compliance risks.

financialSector.title: AI Governance in the Financial Sector
financialSector.p1: In regulated financial environments, AI systems influence credit risk scoring, fraud detection, anti-money laundering processes, and compliance monitoring. These applications directly impact individuals, institutions, and markets.
financialSector.p2: Financial regulators require demonstrable transparency, fairness, and model validation standards. Governance frameworks provide structured workflows, documentation, and reporting mechanisms that ensure models remain defensible and audit-ready.

closing.title: Building Trust Through Structured Governance
closing.description: Effective AI governance transforms advanced systems into transparent, accountable, and resilient decision infrastructures. It bridges research with practical implementation to ensure innovation does not compromise fairness, legality, or public trust. Practical playbooks and implementation templates are planned and will be published to help teams operationalise governance.

lab.title: ML Evaluation Lab
lab.description: Five public datasets. Five decision questions. Explore what recorded evaluations reveal about fairness, model attribution and hypothetical alternatives—and where the evidence stops.
lab.metaDescription: Explore verified lab evaluations on five public ML datasets: fairness, SHAP attribution, counterfactuals, training results and transparent test limitations.
lab.evidenceSubtitle: Selected results from the recorded service run
lab.runTitle: A recorded run, an explicit boundary
lab.runDescription: These are lab evaluations on public datasets, not customer deployments or clinical validation. PASS means the saved response passed the test’s output checks. It does not certify fairness, security or suitability for use.
lab.scenariosDescription: Each scenario connects a model decision to a specific evaluation. Sample sizes refer to the named analysis, not the entire source dataset.
lab.unprivileged: Women in other recorded race categories
lab.alternativeNote: Aggregate summary only; no individual record is shown.
lab.germanExample: All four alternatives changed credit amount and duration; three also changed purpose. Age and sex stayed fixed.
lab.insuranceExample: All three alternatives changed BMI only; the smoking category stayed fixed. This exposes model behavior, not a health recommendation.
lab.undefinedNote: The response returned no defined value for this ratio. It is not zero.
lab.shapScale: Mean absolute SHAP value · model output scale
lab.shapSample: Tree SHAP · {samples} explained samples · {background} background samples
lab.trainingDescription: Measured during the training workflow on held-out test sets on 7 November 2026. These figures are not ML-service evaluation results. Different tasks and datasets are not a model leaderboard.
lab.diabetesWarning: All {count} service tests were not run: TensorFlow was unavailable in the service. There are no recorded attack, defense, privacy or SHAP outcomes for this model.
lab.readingTitle: Read the result and its boundary together

reading.attribution: SHAP assigns contributions to a model’s output; LIME fits a local approximation. Neither establishes why an outcome happens in the world. Rankings depend on the sample, encoding and explainer.
reading.alternatives: DiCE searches for feature combinations that change a prediction. These are model alternatives, not causal interventions, feasible action plans or guarantees of a real outcome.
reading.provenance: The evaluation date is 7 November 2026 (UTC). Results were checked against saved per-test evaluation response bodies and the training manifest. The historical run/report retrieval requests returned HTTP 404; those retrieval endpoints are not used as evidence.
reading.scope: This page contains selected aggregate results and explanatory summaries. Public dataset links identify the recorded sources; the original data, model files and individual records are not distributed here. Values are rounded for display; undefined metrics remain undefined.

adult.title: Adult Income
adult.question: How unevenly is income above $50K represented across the configured protected groups?
adult.methods: Pre- and post-training fairness, global SHAP, local LIME.
adult.interpretation: The pre-training income-label rate is 25.1 percentage points lower in the configured unprivileged intersection, with a favorable-outcome rate 0.23 times that of the privileged intersection. This identifies a disparity in observed labels before model training.
adult.limitations: The comparison is White men versus women in all other recorded race categories. Other sex/race intersections are excluded. This is not a general comparison of all men and women, and it is not a causal or legal finding.
adult.methodology: The processed label dataset is used for pre-training fairness, with income above $50K as the favorable outcome. Sex and race conditions are combined as intersections. Post-training fairness uses the held-out predictions and a separate, sex-only configuration, so the two analyses are not a before/after measure of mitigation. The logistic regression uses a separate preprocessor. Global SHAP used the permutation explainer on 100 samples with 50 background samples; local LIME explained three samples with 1,000 perturbations each.

german_credit.title: German Credit
german_credit.question: Which hypothetical input changes switch a selected credit-risk prediction from bad to good?
german_credit.methods: Local LIME, DiCE classification, global Tree SHAP.
german_credit.interpretation: DiCE generated four alternatives for one selected query, and all four bad-to-good prediction changes were verified against the reloaded model. They illustrate a decision boundary, not a promise of credit approval.
german_credit.limitations: One deliberately selected query cannot represent all applicants. Feature changes may be impractical or incompatible with real lending policy. The model’s good/bad labels are historical dataset labels, not a recommendation about a person.
german_credit.methodology: A random forest with 300 trees, maximum depth 6 and minimum leaf size 20 is evaluated on 200 held-out samples. Genetic DiCE requested four opposite-class alternatives, allowed credit amount, duration, savings category and purpose to vary, and held age and sex immutable. Global Tree SHAP explained all 200 test samples with 50 background samples; LIME explained three samples with 1,000 perturbations each. The recorded source is the Kaggle version containing Risk labels; the originally configured source did not include them.

diabetes.title: Pima Diabetes
diabetes.topic: Security & privacy · service tests not run
diabetes.question: How should robustness and privacy be evaluated for a diabetes classification model?
diabetes.methods: Planned: PGD, HopSkipJump, zeroth-order attack, feature squeezing, membership and attribute inference, SHAP and an automatic SHAP fallback.
diabetes.interpretation: The training workflow measured predictive performance on a held-out test set. The service could not load the Keras model, so this run provides no evidence about its attack resistance, defenses, privacy leakage or service explanations.
diabetes.limitations: The test set contains only 79 samples. Complete-case filtering removes rows with zero-coded missing clinical measurements and can introduce selection bias. This is a public dataset experiment, not clinical validation or a diagnostic tool.
diabetes.methodology: The Keras MLP has 32- and 16-unit hidden layers, dropout 0.3 and L2 regularization 0.001. Normalization is adapted on the fit split only. The 392 complete cases are separated into 250 fit, 63 validation and 79 test samples. Early stopping restored the best weights. The recorded Kaggle mirror replaced an inaccessible original source. All eight service entries are SKIPPED because TensorFlow was unavailable; skipped tests have no evaluated sample count. Membership-inference configuration also lacks supported true-membership labels, so it would require additional evidence before any privacy conclusion.

telco_churn.title: Telco Churn
telco_churn.question: Which encoded features contribute most to the churn model’s output in the evaluated sample?
telco_churn.methods: Global and local Tree SHAP, post-training fairness.
telco_churn.interpretation: Tenure has the largest mean absolute SHAP attribution in the 300-sample global evaluation, followed by the month-to-month contract indicator and the two-year contract indicator. The bars show contribution magnitude, not the direction of change or a causal reason for churn.
telco_churn.limitations: The ranking is specific to the selected sample and model output scale. Contract categories are separate encoded features, not a combined importance score for the original field. Changing a contract does not guarantee retention.
telco_churn.methodology: The CatBoost classifier was trained with depth 6 and early stopping. Global Tree SHAP explained 300 held-out samples with a background of 50; local SHAP explained three selected samples. Post-training fairness used 1,392 held-out predictions and the favorable outcome No churn. Its configured gender/age intersections compare non-senior men with senior women; other intersections are excluded. Attribution and fairness answer different questions.

insurance.title: Medical Insurance
insurance.question: Can the charge model generate hypothetical alternatives within a requested prediction range?
insurance.methods: Global Tree SHAP, DiCE regression, regression fairness.
insurance.interpretation: Three generated alternatives for one selected query reached the requested charge-prediction range. All changed BMI only. This is an illustration of the fitted model’s response surface; it offers no health, pricing or treatment advice.
insurance.limitations: A lower model prediction does not establish that a change is healthy, feasible or will reduce actual charges. Regression fairness compares smoking groups and does not control for other factors. The disparate-impact quantile ratio is undefined in the saved response.
insurance.methodology: The XGBoost regressor uses maximum depth 4, learning rate 0.05 and early stopping. Genetic DiCE requested three alternatives in the range 1,000–5,000 charge units; BMI and smoking category could vary, while age, sex, region and number of children were fixed. Outcomes and changes were verified against the reloaded model. Tree SHAP explained 267 held-out samples with 50 background samples. Fairness used the same 267 predictions: 212 non-smokers and 55 smokers; parity at the median was 0.632, while the impact ratio at the global 0.8 prediction quantile was undefined.
